section_summary: This section documents political, economic, and military developments in Japan between late 1936 and early 1937 following the February 26 Incident. Key despatches and memoranda cover the promulgation of surveillance laws targeting political offenders, the debate and administrative measures surrounding Japan's 'southward advance' policy, labor union suppression in military arsenals, and political corruption scandals such as the indictment of former Railway Minister Uchida. The section culminates in the political crisis of January 1937, tracking the clash between the Army and political parties in the Diet that forced the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet and Prince Saionji's nomination of General Kazushige Ugaki to form a new government.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of a despatch analyzing the consolidation of state authority and Army-guided economic control following the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew observes that although the government's stance against future political assassinations has checked open conspiracy, Army-guided expansion of state control over industry at the expense of private property continues to gain momentum. The despatch emphasizes that the Japanese public adheres deeply to the authority and necessity of government and the Emperor rather than to a fixed socio-economic dogma, making Japan's constitutional structure adaptable to state-directed economic functions. Grew concludes that both the central government and the military emerge reinforced from the February 26 Incident, accelerating pre-existing trends toward total state economic control.
subfiles.title: Despatch on the Political and Economic Consequences of the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Reporting on and enclosing a translation of Law No. 29 providing for the protection and surveillance of persons charged with dangerous thoughts.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Neville transmits an official translation of Law No. 29, promulgated on May 28, 1936, which mandates a two-year period of protection and surveillance for individuals convicted under or charged with offenses against the 1925 Peace Preservation Law. The Embassy explains that the legislation was spurred by the February 26 Incident, as civilian extremists and former military officers involved in past conspiracies—such as Koji Muranaka, Asaichi Isobe, Zei Nishida, and Kazuteru Kita—had previously received lenient or postponed sentences, leaving them free to organize the rebellion. Under the law, competent authorities may restrict offenders' residence, associations, and correspondence, and place them in specialized institutions or under guardian custody. Neville notes that the law applies to both right-wing chauvinists and leftist Communists seeking violent political transformation.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2017: The Law Providing for the Protection and Surveillance of Persons Charged with Dangerous Thoughts

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report and State Department analysis on Japan's 'southward advance' policy, accompanied by Masanori Ito's published articles on naval aspects.
subfiles.summary: This despatch, accompanied by a Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum and clippings from The Japan Times, examines the nature and motives behind Japan's 'southward advance' (nanshin) doctrine. Although Overseas Minister Nagata, Foreign Minister Arita, and Navy Minister Nagano publicly insisted that expansion into Southeast Asia was purely peaceful and economic, the Embassy and Department analysts noted that the concept originated with the Japanese Navy seeking budget parity and prestige comparable to the Army's gains in Manchuria. Concrete implementation measures included the formation of the Taiwan Development Company, the reorganization of the South Seas Development Company, and the appointment of retired Admiral Seizo Kobayashi as Governor General of Formosa. The enclosed three-part treatise by naval commentator Masanori Ito argues that access to the natural wealth and markets of the South Seas is an economic imperative that must be secured through diplomacy, while maintaining naval readiness to defend maritime lifelines.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2019: Japan's 'Southward Advance' Policy

subfiles.about: Analysis of the geopolitical consequences of Japan's surging foreign trade, international trade resistance, and surrounding military defensive rings.
subfiles.summary: This substantive Department of State memorandum assesses the friction caused by Japan's dynamic economic expansion, surging manufacturing exports, and growing population. As foreign nations erect protective tariffs and trade barriers to counter cheap Japanese goods, an 'economic iron ring' is constricting Japan's outward commercial momentum. In parallel, Japanese militarism has led surrounding powers—the Soviet Union, China, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and the United States—to reinforce fortified defensive bastions in Vladivostok, Singapore, Hawaii, and the Philippines, forging a corresponding military iron ring. The memorandum warns that the most vulnerable breach points in this encirclement lie to the south, highlighting China, the Dutch East Indies, and particularly the Philippines once American defense guarantees are withdrawn.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Japan: Economic Developments: Trade: Economic Repercussions and Political Developments and Possibilities

subfiles.about: Reporting the Hirota Cabinet's formal adoption of seven basic national policies and the skeptical reaction of the Japanese press and public.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Dickover reports on the seven fundamental national policies approved by the Hirota Cabinet on August 25, 1936, addressing national defense replenishment, taxation reform, education reform, livelihood stabilization, industrial and trade promotion, Manchukuo policy, and administrative reform. Major Tokyo newspapers criticized the program as overly abstract and devoid of a clear foreign policy toward China and the Soviet Union, with commentators warning that defense expenditures would overshadow all other domestic priorities. The Army's defense replenishment plan alone demands 3.3 billion yen over six years, starting with 300 million yen in the 1937–38 budget. Progress on other key policies, such as the contentious proposal for government control of the electric power industry, remains stalled by complex technical and political debates.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2044: Aftermath of the February 26th Incident

subfiles.about: Reporting on the Japanese Army's prohibition of labor union membership in military arsenals and the resulting political backlash from labor organizations.
subfiles.summary: The despatch analyzes the Army's September 10, 1936 directive ordering 5,600 civilian workers across military arsenals in Osaka, Nagoya, and Kokura to renounce their labor union affiliations in the name of military discipline. Protests were lodged by the Social Mass Party (Shakai Taishuto) and the Labor and Farm Council, which condemned the order as a fascist assault on constitutional rights, but the War Office firmly rejected all petitions by insisting on vertical military control over arsenal personnel. The Army's aggressive stance alarmed the Home Office, which sought to prevent similar union bans from spreading to other government and private factories, while rumors circulated of impending state legislation to outlaw strikes entirely. The controversy intensified friction within the Social Mass Party between nationalist elements favoring cooperation with the military and anti-fascist factions led by Kanju Kato seeking independent proletarian solidarity.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2048: Current Labor Questions Particularly in Their Connection with the Army

subfiles.about: Reporting the arrest and indictment of former Railway Minister Shinya Uchida on charges of receiving bribes.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Dickover reports that Shinya Uchida, Minister of Railways under the Okada Cabinet, was indicted and imprisoned in Ichigaya Prison after questioning by Tokyo procurators uncovered 150,000 yen in suspicious payments from contractors. Because of Uchida's high official status, prosecution proceeded following Imperial consent, with investigators treating the funds as illicit bribes rather than legitimate political campaign donations. The Embassy notes that the public has grown accustomed to corruption in the Railway Ministry, recalling the recent prosecutions of previous ministers Heikichi Ogawa and Chuzo Mitsuchi. While the case does not directly implicate the Hirota Cabinet, it provides anti-parliamentary critics with further ammunition to discredit political parties.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2128: Trial of Former Railway Minister for Bribery

subfiles.about: Transmitting a Chinese editorial analyzing growing friction between the Hirota Cabinet and the Japanese War Office over China policy and domestic reform.
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Peck forwards an English translation of an editorial published in the Nanking journal Hsin Ching Jih Pao on October 13, 1936, analyzing the acute policy dispute between the Hirota Cabinet and the Japanese military. The editorial describes how the War Office capitalized on crises in Shanghai and North China to push for troop deployments, administrative reorganization, and military dominance, clashing with Hirota and civilian ministers who favored diplomatic resolutions. Chinese commentators viewed the tension as an attempt by the military to establish an authoritarian dictatorship, warning that the potential collapse of the Hirota Cabinet would have severe repercussions for Sino-Japanese relations and stability in East Asia.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 264: Summary of Editorial on Japanese Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 2147 concerning Japan's apparent reduction in belligerence toward China and the USSR.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2147, filed in decimal file 793.94/8448. The indexed report investigates an apparent softening of Japan's belligerent posture toward China and the Soviet Union. It questions whether this loss of public and official pugnacity reflects a genuine moderation of foreign policy or a calculated political maneuver orchestrating temporary conciliation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Apparent Lessening of Belligerent Spirit in Japan toward China and the Soviet Union

subfiles.about: Reporting the two-day prorogation of the Imperial Diet following a bitter clash between War Minister Terauchi and Seiyukai member Hamada.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Imperial Diet was prorogued for two days following an acrimonious exchange on the Diet floor between War Minister Hisaichi Terauchi and Kunimatsu Hamada of the Seiyukai. Following the suspension, the War Office issued a defiant midnight statement accusing political parties of obstructing vital post-February 26 nationalistic reforms and failing to comprehend the ongoing international crisis. With parties refusing to submit to military intimidation, the Hirota Cabinet faced either immediate resignation or dissolving the Diet for a general election. Grew interprets the dissolution threat as a government negotiating lever, concluding that although anti-government sentiment is widespread, disunity among political parties would likely ensure that any post-election government remains dominated by the military.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 13: Prorogation of the Imperial Diet and Conflict between the Army and Political Parties

subfiles.about: Brief telegram reporting that Japanese political observers anticipate the imminent dissolution of the Diet and resignation of the Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the State Department that prominent Japanese political figures view the dissolution of the Diet and the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet as virtually inevitable. While awaiting further developments, Grew observes that Japan has successfully navigated severe political crises in the past.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 16: Expected Resignation of the Hirota Cabinet and Diet Dissolution

subfiles.about: Reporting the collective resignation of the Hirota Cabinet due to War Minister Terauchi's intransigence, with General Ugaki mentioned as prospective Premier.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew cables that Prime Minister Hirota tendered the collective resignation of his Cabinet to the Emperor on the afternoon of January 23, 1937. The collapse was triggered by War Minister Terauchi's refusal to accept any compromise with Diet political parties. Although the resignation has not yet been formally accepted and Hirota's successor is not finalized, General Kazushige Ugaki is prominently mentioned for the premiership.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 21: Collective Resignation of the Hirota Cabinet and Candidacy of General Ugaki

subfiles.about: Reporting late news that Genro Prince Saionji has recommended General Kazushige Ugaki to the Throne as the next Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports late-night press coverage by the Tokyo Asahi stating that elder statesman Prince Kimmochi Saionji has recommended General Kazushige Ugaki to the Throne to succeed Hirota as Premier of Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 22: Prince Saionji's Recommendation of General Ugaki for Prime Minister

subfiles.about: Assessing General Ugaki's prospects of establishing a cabinet despite Army resistance, and dismissing rumors of Matsui and Shiratori's appointments.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on high authority that despite vocal Army opposition, General Kazushige Ugaki has a strong likelihood of overcoming military resistance to form a Cabinet, though final arrangements may require several days. Grew also dismisses press rumors that General Matsui will be appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs and Shiratori Vice Minister, characterizing such appointments as unfounded and highly improbable.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 25: Prospects of General Ugaki Forming a Cabinet Despite Army Opposition
